subject: Physics
description: Comprehensive diagnostic question bank for adaptive assessment and knowledge repair.

questions.title: Velocity Direction in Circular Motion
questions.prompt: An object moves in a circle at a constant speed of 10 m/s. Does its velocity remain constant?
options: A) Yes, because the speed is constant at 10 m/s.
B) No, because the direction of motion is continuously changing.
C) Yes, because there is no net force.
D) No, because speed increases around each turn.
questions.rubric: Velocity is a vector possessing both magnitude (speed) and direction. Even if speed is constant, changing direction means velocity is changing.
hints: Remember the definition of a vector quantity.
Does velocity include direction as well as magnitude?

questions.title: Average Velocity vs Average Speed
questions.prompt: A runner completes one full lap around a 400 m circular track in 50 seconds, returning to the starting line. What is the runner's average velocity?
options: B) 0 m/s
questions.rubric: Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time. Returning to the starting point gives a displacement of 0 m, hence average velocity is 0 m/s.
hints: What is the total displacement when returning to the starting point?
Velocity depends on displacement, not distance.

questions.title: Speed Calculation Along Path
questions.prompt: In the same 400 m track lap completed in 50 seconds, what was the runner's average speed?
questions.rubric: Average speed = total distance / total time = 400 m / 50 s = 8 m/s.
hints: Speed is a scalar equal to distance travelled divided by time elapsed.
Divide 400 meters by 50 seconds.

questions.title: Displacement Vector
questions.prompt: A student walks 30 meters East and then 40 meters North. What is the magnitude of the student's net displacement?
questions.rubric: Displacement is the vector from start to finish. Using Pythagoras: sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = sqrt(900 + 1600) = sqrt(2500) = 50 m.
hints: East and North form a right-angled triangle.
Apply the Pythagorean theorem: sqrt(30^2 + 40^2).

questions.title: Acceleration at Projectile Apex
questions.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up into the air. At the exact highest point of its trajectory, what is its acceleration?
options: A) 0 m/s², because the ball is momentarily motionless.
B) 9.8 m/s² downward, because gravity acts continuously.
C) 9.8 m/s² upward, because it was launched upward.
D) Undefined, because velocity is changing signs.
questions.rubric: Even though instantaneous velocity is zero at the peak, gravity continues to exert a downward force of mg, producing a constant downward acceleration of 9.8 m/s².
hints: Does gravity turn off when an object reaches its peak?
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, not the velocity itself.

questions.title: Negative Acceleration and Deceleration
questions.prompt: A car is moving in the negative x-direction and slowing down. What is the sign of its acceleration?
options: A) Negative, because the car is moving in the negative direction.
B) Negative, because slowing down always means negative acceleration.
C) Positive, because the acceleration opposes the negative velocity to slow it down.
D) Zero, because slowing down means losing acceleration.
questions.rubric: If velocity is negative and the object slows down, the change in velocity delta_v is positive, so acceleration is positive.
hints: If velocity is negative (say -20 m/s to -10 m/s), what is delta_v = (-10) - (-20)?
Acceleration direction opposes velocity when slowing down.

questions.title: Linear Acceleration Calculation
questions.prompt: A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s along a straight road in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration in m/s²?
questions.rubric: a = (v_final - v_initial) / t = (30 - 10) / 5 = 20 / 5 = 4 m/s².
hints: Use the formula a = (v - u) / t.
Find the change in velocity first: 30 - 10 = 20 m/s.

questions.title: Mass vs Weight on the Moon
questions.prompt: An astronaut has a mass of 72 kg on Earth. The Moon's gravitational field strength is about 1/6th of Earth's. What is the astronaut's mass on the Moon?
questions.rubric: Mass is the intrinsic measure of an object's inertia and amount of matter, remaining constant regardless of gravitational field strength. Weight changes, but mass is 72 kg.
hints: Distinguish between mass (amount of matter) and weight (gravitational force).
Does mass depend on the local gravitational field?

questions.title: Inertia and Motion in Deep Space
questions.prompt: A spacecraft in deep space runs out of fuel while coasting at 5,000 m/s away from all planets and stars. What will happen to its motion?
options: A) It will gradually slow down and stop as its internal inertia runs out.
B) It will continue moving at 5,000 m/s indefinitely in a straight line.
C) It will immediately stop when the engine stops pushing.
D) It will begin to spiral in place.
questions.rubric: By Newton's first law and the concept of inertia, an object in motion remains in motion at constant velocity unless acted upon by an external net force.
hints: Newton's First Law: what does an object do when net force is zero?
Is inertia a force that runs out, or an inherent property resisting change?

questions.title: Forces Acting on a Book at Rest
questions.prompt: A textbook rests motionless on a flat wooden desk. Which statement correctly describes the forces acting on the book?
options: A) There are no forces acting on the book because it is not moving.
B) Only gravity pulls down; the desk is merely an immovable barrier.
C) Gravity pulls downward and the normal force pushes upward with equal magnitude, balancing to a net force of zero.
D) The downward gravitational force is greater than the upward normal force.
questions.rubric: A motionless object is in static equilibrium: multiple non-zero forces act (downward gravity and upward normal force from the desk), summing to a net force of zero.
hints: Does being at rest mean zero forces act, or that the forces are balanced?
What pushes up against gravity to keep the book from falling through the desk?

questions.title: Net Force with Opposing Forces
questions.prompt: A box of mass 5 kg is pulled to the right with a force of 30 N and pulled to the left with a force of 10 N on a frictionless surface. What is the net force acting on the box?
options: A) 40 N to the right
B) 20 N to the right
C) 30 N to the right
D) 300 N to the right
questions.rubric: Forces are vectors. Opposing collinear forces subtract: F_net = 30 N - 10 N = 20 N in the direction of the larger force (right).
hints: Because the forces point in opposite directions, you must subtract, not add.

questions.title: Net Force in Uniform Motion
questions.prompt: A cargo crate slides across a warehouse floor at a constant velocity of 2 m/s. An electric winch pulls it forward with 150 N. What is the magnitude of the net force on the crate?
options: A) 150 N forward
B) 0 N
C) 75 N forward
D) 300 N forward
questions.rubric: Constant velocity means zero acceleration. By Newton's second law, F_net = m * a = m * 0 = 0 N. Friction exerts 150 N backward, exactly balancing the forward pull.
hints: What is the acceleration of an object moving at constant velocity?
If a = 0, what is F_net = m * a?

questions.title: Newton's First Law Application
questions.prompt: A hockey puck slides across frictionless ice at 5 m/s. How much force is required to keep it moving at this constant speed?
questions.rubric: Newton's First Law states that an object in motion continues in motion with constant velocity unless an external net force acts. Zero net force is required.
hints: Does an object need continuous force to maintain constant velocity on frictionless ice?
Newton's First Law says a net force is only needed to CHANGE motion.

questions.title: Sudden Braking and Inertia
questions.prompt: When a city bus brakes suddenly, standing passengers lurch forward. What physical concept explains this?
options: A) An invisible forward force pushes them when the brakes engage.
B) The passengers' inertia causes them to continue moving forward at their prior velocity while the bus decelerates underneath them.
C) Centrifugal force propels them forward.
D) Air pressure inside the bus surges forward.
questions.rubric: By inertia, passenger bodies maintain their forward velocity until a net braking force is exerted on them. No new forward force is created.
hints: Were the passengers already moving forward before the brakes were tapped?
Their bodies continue moving forward due to inertia.

questions.title: Newton's Second Law Calculation
questions.prompt: A net force of 20 N acts on a cart of mass 4 kg. What is the acceleration of the cart?
questions.rubric: a = F_net / m = 20 N / 4 kg = 5 m/s².
hints: Apply F_net = m * a.
Divide 20 N by 4 kg.

questions.title: Multi-Force Acceleration
questions.prompt: A 10 kg sled is pulled with 50 N East while a friction force of 20 N resists Westward. What is the magnitude of the sled's acceleration?
questions.rubric: Net force = 50 N - 20 N = 30 N East. Acceleration = F_net / m = 30 N / 10 kg = 3 m/s².
hints: Step 1: Calculate the net force by subtracting opposing forces (50 - 20 = 30 N).
Step 2: Divide net force by mass (30 N / 10 kg).

questions.title: Coupled System Acceleration
questions.prompt: Two blocks (m1 = 2 kg and m2 = 3 kg) connected by a light string rest on a frictionless table. A horizontal force of 25 N pulls m2. What is the acceleration of the combined system?
questions.rubric: Total mass = 2 kg + 3 kg = 5 kg. System acceleration = F_net / m_total = 25 N / 5 kg = 5 m/s².
hints: The two blocks accelerate together as one combined system.
Find the total mass first (2 + 3 = 5 kg), then use a = F / m.

questions.title: Action-Reaction Pairs: Bug and Windshield
questions.prompt: A high-speed highway truck collides head-on with a small flying mosquito. How does the magnitude of the force exerted by the truck on the mosquito compare to the force exerted by the mosquito on the truck?
options: A) The truck exerts a vastly larger force because it has much greater mass and momentum.
B) The mosquito exerts a larger force because it gets crushed.
C) The forces have exactly equal magnitude according to Newton's Third Law.
D) The truck exerts a force, but the mosquito exerts zero force.
questions.rubric: By Newton's Third Law, interaction forces between two bodies are always equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The mosquito undergoes massive acceleration because of its tiny mass (a = F/m), not because the force was larger.
hints: Newton's Third Law applies to every interaction regardless of mass difference.
Do not confuse force with the resulting acceleration (damage).

questions.title: Why Action-Reaction Does Not Cancel
questions.prompt: A horse pulls a cart forward. The cart pulls backward on the horse with an equal force. A student asks: 'Why does the cart accelerate if these two forces are equal and opposite?' What is the correct explanation?
options: A) Newton's Third Law only applies once motion ceases.
B) Action and reaction forces act on two DIFFERENT objects, so they never cancel each other out on a single object.
C) The horse's pull is slightly larger than the cart's backward pull during acceleration.
D) Friction eliminates the reaction force entirely.
questions.rubric: Action and reaction forces act on distinct bodies: the horse exerts force on the cart, while the cart exerts force on the horse. To find the cart's acceleration, only forces acting ON the cart are summed.
hints: Which object does the forward pull act on? Which object does the backward pull act on?
Forces can only cancel if they act on the SAME body.

questions.title: Static vs Kinetic Friction
questions.prompt: A heavy wooden crate has a maximum static friction limit of 100 N. A person pushes horizontally with 40 N, and the crate does not budge. What is the magnitude of the static friction force acting on the crate?
questions.rubric: Static friction is an adaptive, responsive force: f_s matches the applied force up to its maximum threshold. Because the crate remains stationary, F_net = 0, so f_s = 40 N.
hints: If the crate remains motionless, what must the net horizontal force be?
Static friction only exerts what is needed to maintain equilibrium, not its maximum 100 N.

questions.title: Friction Direction in Walking
questions.prompt: When a person walks forward on a dry pavement, in which direction does the friction force from the ground act on their shoes?
options: A) Backward, because friction always opposes the direction of overall motion.
B) Forward, because the foot pushes backward against the pavement and static friction pushes forward on the foot.
C) Downward, perpendicular to the pavement.
D) Zero, because walking does not slip.
questions.rubric: The foot attempts to slip backward relative to the ground. Static friction opposes this impending relative slip, pushing forward on the shoe and propelling the walker forward.
hints: Which way does your foot push backward on the floor when stepping?
Static friction opposes RELATIVE motion between surfaces, not necessarily overall body velocity.

questions.title: Linear Momentum Calculation
questions.prompt: A bowling ball of mass 6 kg rolls down an alley with a velocity of 4 m/s. What is its linear momentum in kg·m/s?
questions.rubric: p = m * v = 6 kg * 4 m/s = 24 kg·m/s.
hints: Momentum is mass times velocity (p = m * v).
Multiply 6 by 4.

questions.title: Momentum vs Kinetic Energy Comparison
questions.prompt: A 1000 kg car and a 2000 kg truck both have the exact same linear momentum of 20,000 kg·m/s. Which vehicle has greater kinetic energy?
options: A) Both have identical kinetic energy because their momentums are equal.
B) The 2000 kg truck, because it has twice the mass.
C) The 1000 kg car, because KE = p² / (2m), meaning smaller mass gives larger KE at fixed momentum.
D) Neither vehicle has kinetic energy.
questions.rubric: KE = p² / (2m). Since p is the same, KE is inversely proportional to mass. The car travels at 20 m/s (KE = 200 kJ) while the truck travels at 10 m/s (KE = 100 kJ).
hints: Calculate the speed of each vehicle first (v = p / m).
Car: v = 20 m/s; Truck: v = 10 m/s. Now compute KE = 0.5 * m * v².

questions.title: Conservation of Momentum in Collision
questions.prompt: A 2 kg glider moving at 3 m/s on a frictionless air track collides with and sticks to a stationary 4 kg glider. What is their combined velocity after the collision?
questions.rubric: Total initial momentum = (2 kg * 3 m/s) + 0 = 6 kg·m/s. Total mass after collision = 2 + 4 = 6 kg. v_final = p_total / m_total = 6 / 6 = 1 m/s.
hints: Total momentum before collision equals total momentum after.
p_initial = 2 * 3 = 6 kg·m/s. Combined mass = 6 kg.

questions.title: External Force and Momentum Conservation
questions.prompt: Under what condition is the total linear momentum of a system of particles strictly conserved?
options: A) When there are no internal forces acting between particles.
B) When the net external force acting on the system is zero.
C) Only during perfectly elastic collisions.
D) Whenever total kinetic energy is conserved.
questions.rubric: dp_total / dt = F_net_external. Total momentum is conserved if and only if the net external force on the system is zero.
hints: Internal forces always cancel in pairs via Newton's Third Law.
What kind of net force changes the total momentum of a system?

questions.title: Work Done by Perpendicular Force
questions.prompt: A porter carries a heavy 20 kg suitcase on their shoulder, walking 50 meters horizontally across a flat airport terminal at constant speed. How much mechanical work does the vertical upward lifting force perform on the suitcase during this horizontal walk?
questions.rubric: Work is W = F * d * cos(theta). The lifting force is vertical (theta = 90 degrees relative to horizontal displacement), and cos(90) = 0. Therefore, zero mechanical work is done.
hints: Look at the angle between the vertical lifting force and the horizontal displacement.
W = F * d * cos(90°). What is cos(90°)?

questions.title: Positive and Negative Work
questions.prompt: A crane lowers a 500 N beam vertically downward at a constant velocity through a displacement of 4 meters. What is the work done by the upward tension force in the crane's cable?
questions.rubric: Tension acts upward (theta = 180 degrees relative to downward displacement). W = F * d * cos(180) = 500 N * 4 m * (-1) = -2000 J.
hints: The displacement is downward, but the cable tension pulls upward.
Forces opposing displacement perform negative work.

questions.title: Kinetic Energy Quadratic Scaling
questions.prompt: If a sports car triples its driving speed from 20 m/s to 60 m/s, by what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
questions.rubric: Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of speed: KE = 0.5 * m * v². Tripling speed (3x) multiplies KE by 3² = 9.
hints: Kinetic energy formula: KE = 0.5 * m * v².
What is (3v)² in terms of v²?

questions.title: Kinetic Energy Calculation
questions.prompt: A 2 kg projectile moves at a speed of 10 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in Joules?
hints: KE = 1/2 * m * v².

questions.title: Gravitational Potential Energy
questions.prompt: A 5 kg stone is lifted vertically to a height of 10 meters above the ground (use g = 9.8 m/s²). What is its gravitational potential energy relative to the ground?
questions.rubric: PE = m * g * h = 5 kg * 9.8 m/s² * 10 m = 490 J.
hints: Use PE = m * g * h.
Multiply 5 * 9.8 * 10.

questions.title: Potential Energy Reference Frame
questions.prompt: Can gravitational potential energy have a negative value?
options: A) No, energy is a scalar magnitude and can never be negative.
B) Yes, if the object is located below the arbitrarily chosen zero-reference height.
C) Only in non-gravitational magnetic fields.
D) Only when mass is considered negative.
questions.rubric: Potential energy is defined relative to an arbitrary reference point where PE = 0. If an object is below this reference level, h < 0, giving negative potential energy.
hints: Potential energy depends on the chosen reference datum (h = 0).
If ground level is 0, what is the PE at the bottom of a well?

questions.title: Work-Energy Theorem Application
questions.prompt: A net force of 50 N pushes a 4 kg cart from rest across a smooth floor over a distance of 8 meters. What is the cart's final kinetic energy?
questions.rubric: By the Work-Energy Theorem: W_net = Delta_KE. W_net = F_net * d = 50 N * 8 m = 400 J. Since initial KE = 0, final KE = 400 J.
hints: Work-Energy Theorem: Net work done on an object equals change in kinetic energy.
W_net = F_net * d = 50 * 8 = ?

questions.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
questions.prompt: A 2 kg pendulum bob is released from rest at a height of 5 meters above its lowest point. Ignoring air resistance, what is its speed at the lowest point? (Take g = 10 m/s²)
questions.rubric: Initial mechanical energy = mgh = 2 * 10 * 5 = 100 J. At the lowest point, all PE converts to KE: 0.5 * m * v² = 100 J -> 0.5 * 2 * v² = 100 -> v² = 100 -> v = 10 m/s.
hints: Energy is conserved: initial PE = final KE.
mgh = 0.5 * m * v² => v = sqrt(2gh).

questions.title: Power Calculation
questions.prompt: An electric elevator motor performs 120,000 Joules of work in 60 seconds. What is the power output of the motor in Watts?
questions.rubric: Power = Work / Time = 120,000 J / 60 s = 2,000 W (2 kW).
hints: Power is the rate at which work is done: P = W / t.
Divide 120,000 by 60.

questions.title: Power vs Energy Distinction
questions.prompt: Two weightlifters, Alex and Ben, both lift a 100 kg barbell by 2 meters. Alex completes the lift in 1 second, while Ben takes 3 seconds. Which statement is true?
options: A) Alex does three times more work than Ben.
B) Alex and Ben do identical work, but Alex exerts three times more power.
C) Ben exerts more power because he sustained the force longer.
D) Both exert identical power and work.
questions.rubric: Work depends only on force and displacement (W = mgh is identical). Power is work divided by time: since Alex takes 1/3 the time, Alex develops 3x greater power.
hints: Do both lifters displace the barbell by the same vertical height?
If work is the same, how does time elapsed affect power (P = W / t)?
